title: What Good Ownership Looks Like Day to Day
summary: Owning work means a clear next decision, handoffs someone else can pick up, and honest updates on what you don’t know yet. Being online all day is a different job.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say your team has two people who both "own" things. The first answers every Slack message within a minute, sits in every meeting and has a hand in every open thread. The second replies a bit slower, but their tickets say exactly what's blocked, their handoffs come with a written note, and when they take a week off, the work keeps moving. Ask who the stronger owner is and most people point at the first one. Watch what happens when each of them goes on vacation and the answer flips.

Being everywhere turns you into a bottleneck

It's easy to mistake intensity for ownership. Someone who answers everything, joins everything and absorbs every loose end looks deeply responsible, and for a while it even works. Then the team grows, or that person gets sick for three days, and you find out every decision was routed through one inbox. That's a bottleneck with a friendly face.

GitLab's handbook paints a cleaner picture. Its directly responsible individual (DRI), a term it credits to Apple, is the person "ultimately accountable for the success or failure" of a project. The same page says the DRI has the final say but should consult the relevant people, gather input and divide the tasks (GitLab Handbook). Owning the outcome and doing every piece of the work yourself are two different jobs.

Day to day, a good owner does four things: knows the goal, names the next decision, pulls in the right people and leaves a trail someone else can follow. They don't need to be the hero of every update. They need the work to keep moving with less guessing.

Name the next decision, and who makes it

A lot of stuck work is waiting on a decision, and often nobody realizes they're the one supposed to make it.

Atlassian's DACI play is a handy fix. The Driver gathers the information and gets the decision made by an agreed date. The Approver is "the one person (yes: one!) who makes the decision." Contributors get "a voice, but not a vote," and the Informed hear about it once it's made (Atlassian Team Playbook). You don't need the full template for every choice. One line in the ticket, "Decision: cache or not. Approver: Lan. By: Thursday", turns a vague worry into something people can plan around.

It also helps with the silence that tends to follow a proposal nobody owns (more on that in When Silence in a Team Becomes a Signal). Once people know who decides, they know who to push back on.

Hand off on purpose

Ownership changes hands all the time: someone goes on leave, rotates to another project, finishes an on-call week. Google's SRE book is strict about this during incidents. The incident commander role has to be "clearly handed off at the end of the working day", and the outgoing commander shouldn't leave the call until they get firm acknowledgment that the handoff landed. The rest of the response team is told too, so it's always clear who's leading (Managing Incidents).

Everyday handoffs deserve a lighter version of the same thing. A good handoff note answers four questions:

  • What changed since the last update?
  • What's still open, and which part is riskiest?
  • Where's the evidence: the dashboard, the PR, the thread where the decision was made?
  • Where should the next person start on Monday morning?

Then get an explicit "got it" back. Without that, a handoff is a calendar invite plus a hope that someone's memory fills the gaps.

The handoff test

If you vanished for a week starting now, could someone pick this up from what's written down? If not, you know what your next 15 minutes are for.

Answer what blocks, park what doesn't

A good owner doesn't treat every notification as equally urgent. They answer the question that's blocking someone right now, and they move the debates that only generate heat to a better venue: a design review, a written proposal, Thursday's sync. That protects their focus, and the team's.

A simple rule helps. If a message blocks someone, reply today. If it doesn't, reply when you get to it, and say when that'll be: "This isn't blocking you, right? I'll take a proper look tomorrow morning."

Say what you don't know yet

Owners are tempted to look in control by keeping risks to themselves. That backfires the moment the risk shows up on its own. The stronger move sounds like this: "I don't know yet. I'm checking the payment provider's logs, and I'll come back with two options by 3 p.m." People can plan around that. They can't plan around "should be fine."

Same with dates. Separate what you know from what you're estimating and what's still unknown. "Friday, if the API contract doesn't change" gives people more to work with than "Friday, guaranteed," and it tells them exactly what to keep an eye on.

None of this makes accountability optional. If the work is drifting, the owner says so. If a decision is needed, they ask for it. If a promise can't be kept, they tell the people affected before anyone has to chase them.

Notice the follow-through

Teams get the kind of ownership they celebrate. If the shout-outs go to whoever was online at midnight, you'll get more midnights (and you'll be halfway to the problem in How to Catch Burnout Before It Catches Your Team). Try noticing other things: who made a boundary clearer, who wrote the handoff, who raised a risk while there was still time, who kept a small promise without needing a crisis to do it.

Good ownership ends up looking almost boring. Meetings get shorter. Tickets get clearer. The next person knows where to start. Nobody has to admire the owner for carrying everything, because the owner made the work carryable by more than one person.

Try this week

  • Pick one open item you own and write down the next decision, who approves it and by when.
  • Write a five-line handoff note for something you're carrying, even if you're not going anywhere.
  • Answer one non-urgent message with "not blocking, I'll look tomorrow morning" instead of dropping everything.
  • In your next status update, split things into known, estimated and unknown.
  • Thank one teammate for a clean handoff or a risk they raised early.
